title: Akshay Kumar Stops the Movie at Intermission, Walks Out With Popcorn, and Plays You a Bonus Song
excerpt: 'Welcome To The Jungle' opened today with a 3.75-crore preview and a cheeky post-interval stunt nobody saw coming. Whether the franchise still roars is another question.
body:
The interval slate comes up. The lights, by strict instruction, stay down. And then — instead of the usual scramble for samosas and a leg-stretch — Akshay Kumar strolls onto the screen, popcorn in hand, and addresses you directly. They'd shot a portion of the film, he confesses with a grin, and frankly didn't know where to put it. So they're going to play it now, right here, in the dead zone after the interval slate. Cue the song "Kyun," Akshay and Disha Patani, and a theatre full of people who'd half-risen from their seats sinking back down, laughing.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=R704yP3dlXw https://x.com/akshaykumar/status/2070364268747424044

Forget post-credit scenes. Welcome To The Jungle — Welcome 3, if you're counting — has invented the post-intermission scene, and by every early account it's the most charming three minutes in the film.

"Cue the song "Kyun," Akshay and Disha Patani, and a theatre full of people who'd half-risen from their seats sinking back down, laughing."
"Many viewers, who had got up to rush to the washroom or grab snacks, immediately sat down on hearing Akshay Kumar's message." — a trade source to Bollywood Hungama

!Akshay Kumar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

It is exactly the kind of fourth-wall wink the Welcome franchise was built on: loud, silly, knowingly absurd, and completely uninterested in your notes about logic. Directed by Ahmed Khan, the film landed in cinemas today, June 26, after Thursday-night paid previews that pulled a tidy ₹3.75 crore nett — one of the bigger preview hauls for a Hindi film and an exact echo of Akshay's last outing, Bhooth Bangla. Trade is projecting a roughly ₹15-crore opening day with previews folded in.

The pitch is nostalgia at full volume. Taran Adarsh handed it 3.5 stars and called it a "1980s-style masala entertainer" where the focus is "fun, laughter, nostalgia, and larger-than-life entertainment — not logic or reasoning." Translation: switch your brain to standby and let the ensemble do its thing. And what an ensemble. Akshay Kumar, Suniel Shetty and Paresh Rawal — the holy trinity of the franchise — reunite, joined by Arshad Warsi, Jacqueline Fernandez, Disha Patani, Shreyas Talpade, Rajpal Yadav, Johnny Lever, Tusshar Kapoor, Lara Dutta and, in a reunion 22 years in the making, Raveena Tandon sharing the screen with Akshay again for the first time since Mohra. At 2 hours 45 minutes, there's a lot of jungle to get through.

But here is where the glamour meets the spreadsheet. Behind the scenes, this has been one of the most aggressively engineered releases of the year. Distributors reportedly leaned hard on exhibitors — demanding all shows in several single-screen cinemas, and at least three shows per screen in six-screen multiplexes. That's a confidence play, and also a risk: pile on the showcasing and, if the footfalls don't follow, you're staring at a sea of empty seats by Monday. The interval-stunt instruction to keep the lights down? Same instinct. Control the room, manufacture the moment, protect the experience.

The nervousness underneath the noise is real. Advance booking, by the platform's own read, has been whispering rather than roaring. Comedies live and die on word-of-mouth, and a 1980s-masala throwback in 2026 is a bet that audiences are still hungry for exactly this — no irony, no edge, just Akshay firing a gun from a helicopter and Paresh Rawal doing what Paresh Rawal does. The early-review fans certainly are: one breathlessly clocked the 4-minute-10-second trailer and compared Akshay to Schwarzenegger. The trade is more cautious. Both can be true.

For the diaspora, this is a theatrical-first event and a confident one. Welcome To The Jungle is rolling out wide across North America, the UK and the Gulf this weekend — the Welcome brand travels, and a broad U/A comedy is precisely the kind of film NRI families turn into a Friday-night group outing. No OTT date yet, and with this much riding on the theatrical window, don't expect one announced soon; a streaming landing, likely Prime Video given the ecosystem, is probably eight to ten weeks away.

The honest verdict, on day one: this is review-proof in the way franchise comedies always are. If you grew up on Welcome and Welcome Back, you already know whether you're going. Just do yourself one favour — don't leave at intermission. Akshay's waiting for you out there, popcorn in hand, with a song you didn't know you were getting.
